faq.pageSubtitle: Safety, privacy, and how Collective Will works
faq.safetyQ1: Can I be identified from my submission?
faq.safetyA1: Your submission is linked to a randomly generated ID — not your name, Telegram username, email, or location. We do not log IP addresses. The connection between your identity and your anonymous ID is never exposed.
faq.safetyQ2: Is it safe to participate from inside Iran?
faq.safetyA2: We have designed the platform to minimize what we know about you. That said, we won't tell you it is risk-free — no digital tool is. We recommend using a VPN when accessing the platform or the Telegram bot. Assess your own situation carefully before participating.
faq.safetyQ3: Why do you need my voice?
faq.safetyA3: To ensure one person, one vote. Voice verification exists only to prevent bots and duplicate accounts from distorting the results. It is not used to identify you, and no human ever listens to your recordings.
faq.safetyQ4: What exactly happens to my voice recordings?
faq.safetyA4: You send 3 short voice messages via Telegram. The system converts them into a mathematical fingerprint — a set of numbers that represents acoustic patterns — and then permanently discards the recordings. The fingerprint is encrypted and stored linked only to your anonymous ID. It cannot be reversed to recover your voice, your Telegram account, or your identity.
faq.safetyQ5: Can my voice fingerprint be matched against other databases?
faq.safetyA5: No. The fingerprint we generate is produced by our own system and is not compatible with or exportable to external voice recognition systems.
faq.safetyQ6: What data do you store about me?
faq.safetyA6: An anonymous UUID (random identifier), your encrypted voice fingerprint (irreversible, not linked to your name; encrypted at rest), your submitted concern text (publicly visible, not linked to your name), and your votes (counted anonymously). We do not store your Telegram username, phone number, IP address, or email in connection with your submissions or votes.
faq.howQ1: How does AI organize concerns without editorializing?
faq.howA1: When you submit a concern, an AI model reads the meaning of your text and groups it with other concerns that express similar ideas — regardless of how they're phrased or what language they use. No human decides which concerns are grouped together or which are made more visible. You can inspect every clustering decision in the Audit Trail.
faq.howQ2: Who counts as "the community" that votes?
faq.howA2: Anyone who completes voice verification. We do not require proof of Iranian citizenship or residency. The platform is open equally to Iranians inside Iran and in the diaspora.
faq.howQ3: Can I submit in Farsi, English, or another language?
faq.howA3: Yes. Submit in whatever language feels natural. The AI processes meaning across languages.
faq.howA4: A tamper-evident log of every action in the system — every submission, every clustering decision, every vote count. Anyone can inspect it to verify that results have not been altered.
faq.howQ5: Can concerns be edited or removed after submission?
faq.howA5: Concerns are not edited by anyone after submission. You can request deletion of your own submission by contacting us through the Telegram bot.
faq.aboutA1: An anonymous collective of independent developers and civil society advocates. We have no affiliation with any government, political party, media organization, or foreign state actor.
faq.aboutA2: Some members of our collective are in situations where public association with this project would put them at risk. Anonymity protects them — and it models the same principle we apply to users.
faq.aboutQ3: Can I trust an anonymous team?
faq.aboutA3: You don't have to. The full source code is open at github.com/civil-whisper/collective-will. Every part of the system — how submissions are processed, how voices are handled, how votes are counted — can be independently verified by any developer.
faq.aboutQ4: Is this platform affiliated with any political movement?
faq.aboutA4: No. We have no position on which political outcomes Iranians should want. Our only goal is to give Iranians a trustworthy way to express and aggregate their own views.
faq.aboutQ5: What happens to the final results?
faq.aboutA5: Results are compiled into a public report and published openly. They are available to journalists, researchers, and the international community. We do not filter, editorialize, or selectively publish results.
faq.auditCta: Want to verify everything yourself? Every action is recorded in a tamper-proof chain anyone can inspect.

receiptVerification.title: Receipt Verification
receiptVerification.subtitle: Check whether your action was recorded, published, and externally timestamped.
receiptVerification.independentVerificationBody: Independent reviewers can later download the public bundle, manifest, and OpenTimestamps proof to confirm that the published record matches what the project claims.
receiptVerification.whatThisProvesBody: This shows that your action was recorded by the system and, once published, the public record cannot be changed later without detection.
receiptVerification.whatThisDoesNotProveBody: This does not by itself prove that every possible event was included, or that every system decision was fair. It proves anti-tampering after publication.

verificationGuide.pageSubtitle: A public step-by-step guide for checking the audit trail without requiring everyone to be a programmer.
verificationGuide.whyBody: Most people should not need to read hashes or run terminal commands just to understand whether the public audit trail is trustworthy. This page explains the simple checks first, then keeps the deeper technical path available for journalists, researchers, and developers.

quickSteps.1: Open the daily audit snapshot page for the day you care about.
quickSteps.2: Check whether the snapshot shows a public bundle, a manifest, and an OpenTimestamps proof file.
quickSteps.3: Use the receipt detail page or the public proof endpoint if you want to check whether a specific entry hash appears in that day's bundle.

files.bundle: The bundle is the public redacted record for one day.
files.manifest: The manifest tells you what hash the bundle should have and what timestamping status the day currently has.
files.ots: The .ots file is the detached OpenTimestamps proof for that day's published Merkle root.

auditorSteps.1: Download the bundle, manifest, and .ots proof for a given day.
auditorSteps.2: Recompute the SHA-256 of the downloaded bundle and compare it with manifest.bundle_sha256.
auditorSteps.3: Use the public proof endpoint with an entry hash to check whether that entry is included in the bundle.
auditorSteps.4: Inspect manifest.timestamping.status: stamped means a proof file exists, verified means the proof has been checked against a Bitcoin-backed attestation.
auditorSteps.5: If you want fully independent confirmation, verify the .ots file yourself with the OpenTimestamps client.

verificationGuide.provesBody: It can show that the public record for a given published day was not silently changed later without detection.
verificationGuide.limitsTitle: What this cannot prove by itself
verificationGuide.limitsBody: It does not by itself prove that every possible event was included before publication, or that every system decision was fair.
verificationGuide.costBody: For v0, the project uses public OpenTimestamps calendars because they are effectively free and operationally simple. Self-hosting only makes sense later if the team needs more control or already runs Bitcoin infrastructure.
verificationGuide.advancedBody: These steps are optional. They are here for advanced reviewers who want to verify the proof files outside the website.
verificationGuide.ctaBody: The easiest place to begin is the daily snapshot list, where each day links to its bundle, manifest, and proof files.
